transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-16
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Lina (Redwood Product); Rajesh (NovusAI CTO), Maya (NovusAI ML Eng), Eli (NovusAI Infra)
---
(00:00) Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we, we scheduled an hour to walk through the migration flow from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood — parity mapping, common gotchas, and a quick demo of the API and Console. quick intros?
(00:12) Rajesh: Yeah hi I'm Rajesh, CTO at NovusAI, we run the customer-facing assistant and some retrieval augmented workflows. we're trying to reduce cost and get more control over latency.
(00:22) Maya: Maya, ML Eng, I own the prompt pipelines and the evals, we'll be the ones actually running the migration and tests.
(00:28) Eli: Eli, infra. I'll focus on networking, VPC, and ops.
(00:33) Ava: Great, Samir can you kick off with the parity goals and the mapping approach?
(00:38) Samir: Sure. So the goal is to map existing calls — chat completions, embeddings, streaming responses, function calling — to Redwood API equivalents with minimal code changes and to measure latency/cost parity. we usually produce a mapping sheet that lists the OpenAI/Anthropic/Together endpoint, the Redwood endpoint, SDK snippet, and notes about behavior differences. e.g., OpenAI ChatCompletion -> Redwood /v1/chat or sdk.chat.create, Anthropic assistant-style -> Redwood chat mapping as well.
(01:10) Maya: how about function calling? we use OpenAI function calling heavily to structure outputs.
(01:15) Samir: Redwood supports structured function/tool calling too; the mapping is straightforward, though the names and the exact call shape are a bit different in the SDK. we'll show a code snippet. important bits: signal for partial streaming, and also how Redwood handles tool response truncation and error signals.
(01:34) Lina: also note quantization/latency differences — for some Together models you get different throughput characteristics. we provide performance profiles per model in the catalog.
(01:46) (02:05) Rajesh: could you show a live example of an OpenAI -> Redwood mapping? like with a small prompt and stream?
(02:10) Samir: yep, i'll share my screen.
(02:18) (screen shares, small pause, some background typing)
(03:05) Samir: ok here's a typical OpenAI call: openai.chat.completions.create({model: 'gpt-4o', messages: [...] , stream: true}) and the equivalent on Redwood is client.chat.create({model: 'redwood-v2', input: messages, stream: true}) — you can see the param names are slightly different: input vs messages, and Redwood uses model aliases like redwood-v2, rw-small for smaller models. we provide an adapter snippet in the mapping sheet to do a 1-for-1 shim.
(03:50) Maya: what about tokens counting? our billing dashboards are token-count-sensitive.
(03:56) Samir: Redwood exposes token usage in the response and in the Console. note: tokenization can differ slightly across models; we recommend running a tokenization parity script we include with the mapping to compare counts for your prompt set.
(04:20) Ava: Lina, can you jump into the Console demo — cost and trace views?
(04:26) Lina: yeah. switching to Console. this is the per-route latency breakdown — you can filter by model, tenant, or path. we show token-level cost, cache hit rate, and KV cache stats. for migrations we often set up a canary route to route 5-10% of traffic to Redwood to compare live quality and cost.
(05:00) Rajesh: we rely on prompt-level caching in our OpenAI setup; do you support prefix caching?
(05:07) Samir: yes, Redwood supports prefix/KV caching that is request-aware, and we can map your existing cache key scheme. the Console shows cache hit rate and savings. Optimize will also make batching and caching recommendations per workload.
(05:30) (05:45) Eli: for Dedicated or Private deployments we need SSA/contractual SLA numbers and KMS integration, like HSM support.
(05:52) Ava: yep we'll share the enterprise pack docs. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS, HSM integrations, and keeps audit logs for compliance. we also have SOC2 and ISO summaries in the security pack.
(06:10) Maya: one concern is model behavior differences — hallucinations and output style. how do you support evals/regressions?
(06:18) Lina: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring tied to prompt sets. you run your evals, baseline them on current models, and Optimize alerts on regression. plus you can pin model versions and roll back automatically if quality dips.
(06:35) (07:00) Samir: quick note on streaming semantics: Redwood streams tokens similarly to OpenAI but frames events slightly differently — e.g., partial token payloads, then delta updates. our SDK has a drop-in streaming client and an adapter layer for typical OpenAI streaming handlers. some minor switch code but usually 10-20 lines.
(07:25) Rajesh: show me cost examples — we pay X right now on OpenAI for embeddings and chat.
(07:30) Ava: we asked for your usage breakdown before the call and we have an estimated ballpark. for example, for your chat-heavy routes with average 80 tokens in prompt and 150 tokens in outputs, Redwood hosted could be ~20-30% lower per-token cost; Dedicated more if you commit. we'll send the detailed pricing.
(07:58) (08:12) Maya: embeddings — we use OpenAI embeddings for vector store. how's compatibility and dimensionality?
(08:18) Samir: Redwood hosts multiple embeddings models including open-compatible dims; we catalog approximate similarity and provide migration utilities to re-embed or use hybrid approaches. note: similarity behavior varies by model, so we recommend A/B tests.
(08:40) Ava: ok next demo: show code adapter and a demo of a canary rollout in Console.
(08:47) Samir: walking through adapter repo — we have a node/python shim that converts openai.ChatCompletion shape to Redwood SDK. code example:
(09:05) // OpenAI
// openai.chat.completions.create({ model: 'gpt-4o', messages: msgs })
// Redwood shim
// client.chat.create({ model: mapModel('gpt-4o'), input: msgs })
(09:30) Samir: mapModel will translate model alias and apply recommended params (temp, max_tokens) and sometimes switch to quantized variant for Dedicated.
(09:45) Maya: will this preserve function calling?
(09:48) Samir: yes, we shim the functions array and responses are delivered in the same structured format after minor name changes. we include tests asserting function call presence.
(10:02) (10:30) Rajesh: latency — we need p95 under 300ms for short queries. can you hit that?
(10:36) Samir: it depends on model size and deployment mode. for rw-small on hosted you can see p95 ~80-120ms on simple prompts; for larger models, dedicated pools and pinning give more predictable p95. we also discussed prefix cache and batching to keep p95 down. we'll run benchmarks with your payload.
(11:05) Eli: networking — for Private we need VPC peering and static egress IPs for allow-lists.
(11:12) Ava: yes Private supports customer VPC options and on-prem packages. we can provide architectural docs for peering and NAT/static IPs.
(11:25) (11:40) Maya: any gotchas with KV cache or session state? we maintain long LLM conversations persisted in our DB and use KV cache to speed up token regen.
(11:49) Samir: Redwood's KV cache stores key/value per-tenant and can be synced; there are TTLs and size limits to tune. it will reduce token usage when you have repeated prefixes. mapping wise, just ensure your session ids map to Redwood conversation ids. we can help instrument that in the parity script.
(12:15) (12:45) Samir: ok now a quick peek at Optimize: it will analyze request traces, suggest batching windows, quantization profiles and when to move a route to a cheaper model while constraining quality drift. here's an example report that suggests using rw-quant-small for the low-priority notification route and keep redwood-v2 for core end-user flows.
(13:05) Rajesh: can Optimize suggest quantization per GPU type? we run on A100 and some Ampere instances.
(13:12) Lina: Optimize recommendations are hardware-aware — it will recommend kernels/quantization that match the underlying hardware and give expected latency/cost deltas.
(13:28) (13:50) Eli: security docs, we need encryption in transit and at rest, key rotation policy, and audit trails.
(13:57) Ava: we'll share the security pack PDF and onboarding checklist. Private includes customer-managed KMS and full audit logs; Hosted supports enterprise KMS and encryption at rest.
(14:15) Maya: for migration timeline we have a Q4 target. can we get an estimate for how long a pilot would take?
(14:22) Samir: typical pilot (canary + benchmarks + evals) takes 3-6 weeks depending on test coverage. given your usage, I'd say closer to 4 weeks: week 1 mapping and setup, week 2 canary and comparisons, week 3 evals and regression tuning, week 4 decision and scaling.
(14:45) Rajesh: good. cost vs accuracy tradeoffs — we'll need to see regression alerts before we move any production traffic.
(14:53) Lina: absolutely, we can gate rollouts on eval thresholds and automatic rollback.
(15:05) (15:30) Samir: quick demo of the parity mapping spreadsheet — columns: source_endpoint, source_model, target_endpoint, target_model, adapter_snippet, expected_token_delta, notes. we'll populate a few of your real routes after you share the CSV.
(15:50) Rajesh: we'll share a usage CSV by Monday.
(15:55) Ava: great, that'll let Samir run an initial cost/latency estimate.
(16:05) (16:20) Maya: what's the effort to re-embed our corpus if we switch embeddings?
(16:26) Samir: re-embedding depends on size — for 5M docs it's a non-trivial job; we recommend incremental re-embedding and hybrid similarity during the transition. Optimize can prioritize which shards to re-embed first based on query traffic.
(16:50) Eli: would Dedicated help with token costs?
(16:55) Ava: Dedicated is reserved capacity — if you commit, unit costs drop significantly and you get predictable throughput. we'll model this in the pricing sheet.
(17:10) (17:30) Rajesh: any references or customers who've migrated from Together?
(17:35) Ava: yes we've done migrations from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together. I'll share case studies and a benchmark deck.
(17:45) Maya: ok let's look at an edge case — streaming + tools + embeddings in a single workflow.
(17:52) Samir: demonstrates a typical RAG pipeline: user prompt -> retrieval (embedding lookup) -> system constructs tool calls for external search -> chat model streams answer and calls tool outputs. The mapping works; you need to wire the tool output parser to Redwood's tool call schema. we have sample code.
(18:30) (18:50) small cross-talk and brief interruption, minor audio glitch (transcription note: 'red wood' sometimes split)
(19:05) Ava: we're at about 40 minutes in, any other blockers?
(19:10) Rajesh: main blockers: security review, pricing for committed Dedicated, and an end-to-end benchmark with our prompt set.
(19:18) Ava: actionable — we'll send security docs, pricing, and Samir will run the benchmark/test.
(19:25) (19:40) Samir: i'll need your CSV and a small test harness — we'll run hosted + dedicated variants. results will include p50/p95, token usage and cost delta, plus qualitative eval metrics.
(20:00) Maya: timeline looks good.
(20:05) Ava: ok recap and next steps: share parity sheet, pricing, run benchmarks, schedule security deep dive. who owns what we listed earlier.
(20:18) Rajesh: thanks, appreciate it.
(20:22) Ava: thanks everyone. we'll follow up by Friday with the docs and sample mapping.
(20:30) (call ends, recording stops)
